title: The 0500 Course at a Glance
description: How IGCSE First Language English 0500 (2027–2029) is built: the two papers, their questions, marks and word limits, the assessment objectives, command words, and how 0500 differs from 0990 and 0510/0511.

notes.heading: The Two-Component Structure
notes.body: Every candidate takes two components, each worth 50% of the qualification. Paper 1 Reading is a 2-hour written paper of 80 marks. Alongside it you take either Paper 2 Directed Writing and Composition (2 hours, 80 marks) or Component 3, a Coursework Portfolio of three assignments (writing to discuss, argue or persuade for 30 marks, to describe for 25, and to narrate for 25), internally assessed and externally moderated. Component 4, the Speaking and Listening Test, is optional: it is separately endorsed with grades 1 (high) to 5 (low), and its marks never count towards your written grade. The written components are graded A* to G. In other words, the whole qualification is two 80-mark halves — one mostly about reading, one mostly about writing.

illustration.alt: Structure diagram of the 0500 exam: Paper 1 Reading with its four 20-mark questions and word limits beside Paper 2 Directed Writing and Composition with Section A and Section B, plus a strip noting the coursework alternative and the optional speaking test.
illustration.caption: Two 2-hour papers of 80 marks each. Paper 1 asks four compulsory 20-mark questions on three texts; Paper 2 splits into Directed Writing (Section A) and Composition (Section B).

notes.heading: Paper 1 at a Glance
notes.body: Paper 1 is 2 hours, 80 marks, and every candidate answers the same four compulsory questions on three reading texts printed on an insert. The texts total roughly 1400 words, and you should spend about 15 minutes reading them; dictionaries are not allowed. Question 1 Comprehension (20 marks, Text A) is a series of short-answer sub-questions testing all five reading objectives. Question 2 Summary task (20 marks, Text B) splits into 2(a), a selective summary in your own words written as continuous prose of no more than 120 words (10 reading marks plus 5 writing marks), and 2(b), a short-answer question on attitudes and opinions (5 marks). Question 3 (20 marks, Text C) combines short-answer sub-questions (10 marks) with a language task of 200–250 words (10 marks). Question 4 Extended response to reading (20 marks, Text C) asks for 250–300 words in one of six text types — letter, report, journal, speech, interview or article — and is worth 10 reading marks plus 10 writing marks.

notes.heading: Paper 2 at a Glance
notes.body: Paper 2 is 2 hours, 80 marks, in two sections, and you answer one question from each. Section A Directed Writing (40 marks) is built on one or two texts totalling 550–650 words. Question 1(a) is a short structured question in which you analyse, evaluate and show your understanding of the text(s) — just 5 marks, testing R3 and R4. Question 1(b) asks you to use, develop and evaluate the material in a discursive, argumentative or persuasive speech, letter, article or report of about 250–350 words, worth 10 reading marks plus 25 writing marks. Section B Composition (40 marks) offers a choice of four titles — two descriptive and two narrative — and you write about 350–450 words; all 40 marks are writing marks (W1 to W5). Note where the prizes sit: the 25 writing marks on 1(b) and the 40 on the composition are where accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar (W5) are assessed on this paper, so protect checking time.

notes.heading: The Assessment Objectives: R1–R5 and W1–W5
notes.body: Every mark you can earn belongs to a named assessment objective, and the syllabus prints them next to each question. Reading: R1 demonstrate understanding of explicit meanings; R2 demonstrate understanding of implicit meanings and attitudes; R3 analyse, evaluate and develop facts, ideas and opinions, using appropriate support from the text; R4 demonstrate understanding of how writers achieve effects and influence readers; R5 select and use information for specific purposes. Writing: W1 articulate experience and express what is thought, felt and imagined; W2 organise and structure facts, ideas and opinions for deliberate effect; W3 use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures appropriate to context; W4 use language appropriate to purpose and to engage the audience; W5 make accurate use of spelling, punctuation and grammar. The weighting matters strategically: Paper 1 is 80% reading and 20% writing; Paper 2 is 20% reading and 80% writing; overall the qualification is 50/50. So even in the 'reading' paper, 15 of the 80 marks — 2(a)'s five plus Question 4's ten — reward how well you write.

notes.heading: Command Words: What the Question Is Really Asking
notes.body: The syllabus lists eleven command words, and each one signals the depth expected. Identify means name, select or recognise — a short, precise answer. Give means produce an answer from the text or memory. Outline means set out the main points. Describe means state the points of a topic or give characteristics and main features. Explain means set out purposes or reasons, say why or how, and support with relevant evidence. Analyse means examine in detail to show meaning, identifying elements and the relationships between them. Evaluate means judge the quality, importance or value of something. Assess means make an informed judgement. Justify means support a case with evidence or argument. Consider means review and respond to given information. Suggest means apply your understanding to propose an answer where several could be valid. Read the command word together with the mark tariff: 'identify' for 1 mark wants a phrase; 'explain' for 3 marks wants a point, its reasoning and support.

notes.heading: What Changed for 2027–2029
notes.body: This syllabus is for first examination in 2027 (June and November series, plus March in India); the previous window was 2024–2026, and older revision guides describe a different paper. The total marks and durations are unchanged, but Paper 1 has been restructured into four compulsory questions of 20 marks each based on three texts in an insert. Question 1 is now 20 marks and tests all five reading objectives. Question 2 gained a new 5-mark part 2(b) on attitudes and opinions, so the summary task is now 15 reading plus 5 writing marks. Question 3 now includes 2 marks for showing you understand identified words, bold type replaces underlining, and the language task has been shortened to 200–250 words. Question 4 is now 10 reading plus 10 writing marks at 250–300 words. On Paper 2, the Section A texts were reduced to 550–650 words and the task was split in two: the new 1(a) is worth 5 marks and assesses R3 and R4 — R4 was not previously assessed on this paper — while 1(b) carries 10 reading and 25 writing marks. The composition titles are unchanged; marking criteria throughout were updated. The objective wording was refreshed, but Cambridge states the skills assessed have not changed.

notes.heading: Which Syllabus Are You Actually On?
notes.body: Similar code numbers hide very different qualifications, so check yours before using any revision material. 0500 is First Language English, graded A* to G. 0990 is the same content graded 9 to 1 for UK schools — nothing else differs. 0510 and 0511 are English as a Second Language, a different qualification for learners whose first language is not English; never prepare for 0500 with 0510 materials. Also distinct are 0472 (English as an Additional Language) and 1123 (O Level English Language). You cannot combine 0500 with any of those in the same exam series. Private candidates should note that some components are not available to them. Once you know you are on 0500, use this course's topics in order: each Paper 1 question type and each Paper 2 section gets its own topic, with the mark tariffs, word limits and examiner expectations taught one at a time.

flashcards.definition: 2-hour written paper, 80 marks, 50% of the qualification. Four compulsory 20-mark questions on three texts totalling about 1400 words, with about 15 minutes' reading time.
flashcards.example: Q1 Comprehension, Q2 Summary task, Q3 Short answers + language task, Q4 Extended response.

flashcards.definition: 2-hour written paper, 80 marks, 50% of the qualification. Section A Directed Writing (40 marks, based on texts of 550–650 words) plus Section B Composition (40 marks, one of four titles).
flashcards.example: 1(a) analysis for 5 marks; 1(b) a speech, letter, article or report of 250–350 words; composition of 350–450 words.

flashcards.definition: The alternative to Paper 2: three assignments (argue/persuade 30 marks, describe 25, narrate 25), internally assessed and externally moderated.
flashcards.example: A school might offer coursework instead of the timed second paper; the marks weighting stays 50%.

flashcards.definition: An optional, separately endorsed test (individual talk plus conversation) graded 1 (high) to 5 (low); its marks never contribute to the written grade.
flashcards.example: A candidate can hold a grade A in 0500 and a separate endorsed grade 2 for speaking and listening.

flashcards.definition: The selective summary is continuous writing in your own words of no more than 120 words — 10 reading marks (R1, R2, R5) plus 5 writing marks (W1, W2, W3).
flashcards.example: Writing 200 words wastes time and breaks the task's rules; the limit is 120.

flashcards.definition: A response of 200–250 words on how the writer uses language in Text C; 10 marks testing R1, R2 and R4 — all reading marks.
flashcards.example: Analysing three or four powerful words or phrases and their effects.

flashcards.definition: 250–300 words in one of six text types — letter, report, journal, speech, interview or article — responding to Text C; 10 reading marks plus 10 writing marks (W1–W4).
flashcards.example: Write a journal entry as one of the people described in Text C, using its details.

flashcards.definition: Demonstrate understanding of how writers achieve effects and influence readers.
flashcards.example: Explaining how a writer's word choice makes a place feel threatening.

flashcards.definition: Make accurate use of spelling, punctuation and grammar. Assessed in Paper 2 (1b and the composition) and in coursework — not among Paper 1's writing marks.
flashcards.example: Leaving five minutes to check the composition for comma splices protects W5 marks.

flashcards.definition: Examine in detail to show meaning, identifying elements and the relationships between them — the deepest level of response on the list.
flashcards.example: Analyse how the writer builds tension: break the passage into choices and trace how they combine.

flashcards.definition: Name, select or recognise — signals a short, precise answer with no development needed.
flashcards.example: Identify two things the writer dislikes about the journey: two phrases are enough.

flashcards.definition: 0500 is First Language English graded A*–G; 0990 is the same content graded 9–1; 0510/0511 are English as a Second Language — a different qualification entirely.
flashcards.example: Using a 0510 past paper to revise for 0500 trains the wrong exam.

questions.stem: How long is Paper 1, and how many marks is it worth?
choices: 2 hours; 40 marks
1 hour 30 minutes; 80 marks
2 hours; 80 marks
2 hours 30 minutes; 100 marks
questions.explanation: Paper 1 Reading lasts 2 hours and carries 80 marks — half the qualification. The 40-mark figure belongs to each section of Paper 2, not to Paper 1, and neither 1 hour 30 minutes nor 100 marks appears anywhere in this syllabus.

questions.stem: A student plans to skip Question 2 on Paper 1 to leave more time for Question 4. What is wrong with this plan?
choices: All four questions are compulsory, so skipping one throws away 20 of the 80 marks
Nothing — candidates may choose any three of the four questions
Question 2 is worth more marks than Question 4
Only Question 1 is compulsory; the rest are optional
questions.explanation: Paper 1 has no choice: all four questions are compulsory and each is worth 20 marks, so omitting one caps the paper at 60 before marking even begins. Every question carries the same 20 marks, so no question outranks another, and the paper offers no optional sections.

questions.stem: Which statement about Question 2(a) is accurate?
choices: You may quote freely from the text because only reading skills are assessed
You should write about 200–250 words of continuous prose
It is a summary of Text C in note form
It is a selective summary of Text B in your own words, in continuous writing of no more than 120 words, worth 10 reading marks and 5 writing marks
questions.explanation: 2(a) is a selective summary based on Text B, written in your own words as continuous prose of no more than 120 words; it carries 10 reading marks (R1, R2, R5) and 5 writing marks (W1, W2, W3). The 200–250 word figure belongs to the Question 3 language task, the summary is on Text B not Text C, and because writing marks are at stake, lifting phrases wholesale works against you.

questions.stem: Component 4, the Speaking and Listening Test…
choices: is compulsory for all 0500 candidates
is optional and separately endorsed — its marks never count towards the overall grade
contributes 20% of the final grade
replaces Paper 2 for candidates who prefer speaking
questions.explanation: Component 4 is optional and separately endorsed with grades 1 (high) to 5 (low); its marks do not contribute to the written grade at all. It is neither compulsory nor a substitute for Paper 2 — the only alternative to Paper 2 is the Component 3 coursework portfolio.

questions.stem: In Paper 2 Section B, a candidate must…
choices: answer one descriptive title and one narrative title
write about 250–350 words
choose one title from four — two descriptive and two narrative — and write about 350–450 words
respond to the printed texts from Section A
questions.explanation: Section B offers four titles, two descriptive and two narrative; you choose one and write about 350–450 words for 40 writing marks. Answering two titles halves your time for each and is not what is asked, 250–350 words is the length of Section A 1(b), and the composition is free writing with no printed stimulus — the texts belong to Section A.

questions.stem: Which objective is defined as 'demonstrate understanding of implicit meanings and attitudes'?
choices: R2
R1
R3
R5
questions.explanation: R2 covers implicit meanings and attitudes — what the text suggests rather than states. R1 is explicit meanings only, R3 is analysing, evaluating and developing ideas with textual support, and R5 is selecting and using information for specific purposes.

questions.stem: A friend says: 'The Question 3 language task is a writing task, so spelling and punctuation are marked there.' Why is this wrong?
choices: It is actually right — every extended answer on both papers tests W5
The language task also tests R3, which covers accuracy
Spelling and punctuation are marked in Question 4 instead
The language task's 10 marks are all reading marks (R1, R2, R4); W5 accuracy is assessed in Paper 2's 1(b) and the composition
questions.explanation: The syllabus assigns the language task 10 reading marks against R1, R2 and R4 only — no writing marks at all. W5 (accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar) is assessed in Paper 2's 1(b) and the Section B composition, and Question 4's writing marks are W1–W4, which still exclude W5. Clear expression always helps, but the tariff here rewards reading, not technical accuracy.

questions.stem: The command word 'identify' tells you to…
choices: write a developed paragraph with evaluation
name, select or recognise — a short, precise answer is expected
give your own opinion with justification
copy a full paragraph from the text
questions.explanation: Identify means name, select or recognise: the answer is short and precise, usually a word or phrase. Developed paragraphs and personal opinions belong to analyse, evaluate or justify questions, and copying whole paragraphs is poor evidence selection under any command word.

questions.stem: Paper 2 Section A Question 1(b) requires you to…
choices: summarise the printed text(s) in no more than 120 words
analyse how the writer uses language, and nothing else
use, develop and evaluate the ideas in the text(s) in a discursive, argumentative or persuasive speech, letter, article or report of about 250–350 words
invent a narrative unrelated to the printed text(s)
questions.explanation: 1(b) is directed writing: you take the material in the text(s), develop it and evaluate it in one of four forms — speech, letter, article or report — at about 250–350 words, for 10 reading and 25 writing marks. The 120-word summary is Paper 1's Question 2(a), pure language analysis is the Paper 1 language task, and ignoring the stimulus wastes the 10 reading marks for using it.

questions.stem: What is genuinely new in Paper 2 for first examination in 2027?
choices: Question 1(a) — a 5-mark structured question assessing R3 and R4, an objective not previously assessed on this paper
The Section B composition — it is a brand new task
The 80-mark total for the paper
The two-hour duration
questions.explanation: For 2027 the Directed Writing task was split: the new 1(a) is a 5-mark structured question testing R3 and R4, and R4 had not previously been assessed on Paper 2. The composition tasks are explicitly unchanged, and both the 80-mark total and the 2-hour duration carried over from the previous syllabus — so only 1(a) is new.

questions.stem: A school in the UK enters its students for syllabus 0990 instead of 0500. What changes for those students?
choices: 0990 is an easier qualification aimed at second-language learners
0990 has no written papers
The content is completely different from 0500
Only the grading scale — 0990 reports grades 9–1 instead of A*–G; the content and assessment are the same
questions.explanation: 0990 is Cambridge IGCSE (9–1) First Language English: the same content as 0500, reported on the 9–1 scale used in UK schools. It is not a second-language course (that is 0510/0511), it has the same written assessment structure, and the content does not differ — only the grade scale does.

questions.stem: How much reading time does the syllabus advise for Paper 1, and how long are the three texts combined?
choices: About 5 minutes; roughly 800 words
About 15 minutes; roughly 1400 words
About 30 minutes; roughly 2000 words
There is no recommended reading time
questions.explanation: The syllabus advises spending about 15 minutes reading the three texts, which total roughly 1400 words. Five minutes is not enough to annotate three texts, 30 minutes would consume a quarter of the paper before you write a word, and the syllabus does give explicit guidance, so the unlimited-time option is wrong.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the text types offered for Question 4's extended response?
choices: Journal
Speech
Poem
Report
questions.explanation: Question 4 offers six text types: letter, report, journal, speech, interview and article. Journal, speech and report are all on that list; poem is not — poetry is never a required form on this paper.

questions.stem: Why does Paper 1 — 'the reading paper' — award writing marks in Questions 2(a) and 4?
choices: Overall the qualification weights reading and writing 50/50; Paper 1 is 80% reading but 20% of its marks reward how well you write
It is a printing error in the syllabus
The writing marks only reward neat handwriting
All 80 marks on Paper 1 are reading marks
questions.explanation: The qualification is weighted 50% reading and 50% writing overall, and Paper 1's weighting is 80% reading and 20% writing — 2(a) carries 5 writing marks (W1–W3) and Question 4 carries 10 (W1–W4). Handwriting is not assessed, and the mark splits are printed in the syllabus, so the 'error' and 'all reading' options both fail.

questions.stem: A student revises from a guide written for the 2024–2026 syllabus. Which piece of its advice is now dangerous?
choices: 'Paper 1 lasts two hours' — the duration has changed
'The paper is worth 80 marks' — the total has changed
'The composition titles work the same way' — they have been replaced
'Write a language analysis of 300 words or more' — the task is now 200–250 words, so this wastes time and encourages padding
questions.explanation: For 2027 the language task was reduced to 200–250 words, so an old guide pushing 300+ words trains the wrong response. The other three pieces of advice are still true: Paper 1 remains 2 hours and 80 marks, and the composition tasks are explicitly unchanged — the trap is that much of the old guide remains valid, which makes its outdated parts harder to spot.
